name: Jack Kornfield
ruleBreak: Rejected the idea that Buddhist meditation required monastic renunciation or religious conversion. In the 1970s, serious meditation meant shaving your head and joining a monastery. Kornfield trained as a monk in Thailand under Ajahn Chah, then came back to America, got a PhD in clinical psychology, and taught vipassana as a practical skill for laypeople with jobs, families, and mortgages.
twoWorlds: Theravada Buddhist monasticism meets Western clinical psychology. He was an ordained forest monk in Thailand and Burma, then earned a PhD in clinical psychology, becoming one of the first people to bridge rigorous Buddhist contemplative training with the language and frameworks of Western psychotherapy.
stupidSimplicity: The heart is already whole — meditation just clears what's in the way.
remarkableResult: Co-founded two of the most influential meditation centers in the West: Insight Meditation Society (1975) and Spirit Rock (1987). Authored 16 books selling over 2 million copies in 20 languages. Has been teaching continuously since 1974, over 50 years, training thousands of Western meditation teachers.

name: Ram Dass
ruleBreak: Rejected the Western academic framework for understanding consciousness. As Dr. Richard Alpert, he was a Harvard psychology professor running psilocybin experiments. When Harvard fired him, instead of defending his academic credentials, he abandoned his entire Western identity, went to India, and came back as Ram Dass — a devotee, not a professor.
twoWorlds: Harvard psychology and psychedelic research meets Hindu devotional practice (bhakti yoga). He went from being Dr. Richard Alpert, tenured professor conducting controlled LSD experiments at one of the world's most prestigious universities, to sitting at the feet of Neem Karoli Baba in India, merging psychedelic inquiry with ancient devotional surrender.
stupidSimplicity: Be here now.
remarkableResult: Be Here Now (1971) sold over 2 million copies and became the counter-culture bible that introduced an entire generation to Eastern spirituality. Influenced Steve Jobs, George Harrison, and Wayne Dyer. Created the template that every Western spiritual teacher since has followed: go East, come back, translate.

name: Vishen Lakhiani (Mindvalley)
ruleBreak: Rejected the traditional education model that separates personal growth from professional development. While universities taught hard skills and self-help stayed on the bookshelf, Vishen built Mindvalley as a platform that treats meditation, emotional intelligence, and biohacking as serious education, delivered with Silicon Valley production quality and gamification.
twoWorlds: Silicon Valley tech entrepreneurship meets Eastern meditation and personal growth. He was a burnt-out computer engineer at a tech startup who discovered meditation at 26 to manage his stress, then applied tech-startup thinking (rapid iteration, gamification, community platforms) to transform personal development into a scalable digital education business.
stupidSimplicity: Most of what you were taught about success is a 'brule' (bullshit rule) — question everything you inherited.
remarkableResult: Built Mindvalley from $700 in startup capital to a company reaching over 20 million students in 80+ countries. His book 'The Code of the Extraordinary Mind' became a New York Times bestseller. Created a model where world-class teachers (from neuroscientists to monks) deliver structured personal growth curricula online.

name: Marianne Williamson
ruleBreak: Rejected the idea that spirituality and social action are separate domains. While most spiritual teachers stayed in meditation halls and most activists stayed in the streets, Williamson took A Course in Miracles — a dense channeled spiritual text from the 1970s — and applied it directly to AIDS activism, politics, and feeding the sick. She later ran for president.
twoWorlds: 1970s New Age spirituality (A Course in Miracles) meets frontline social activism and politics. She was a spiritual teacher lecturing on forgiveness and miracles who simultaneously founded Project Angel Food during the AIDS crisis and eventually ran for the US presidency, refusing to separate inner work from outer service.
stupidSimplicity: Love is what we were born with. Fear is what we learned here.
remarkableResult: A Return to Love spent 39 weeks on the NYT bestseller list, hit #1 on Publishers Weekly for 11 weeks, sold over 1.5 million copies. Founded Project Angel Food, which has delivered over 14 million free meals to people with life-threatening illnesses. Named by Oprah as a defining spiritual voice of her generation.

name: Michael Beckwith
ruleBreak: Rejected the idea that spiritual community requires subscribing to a single religious doctrine. While most churches demanded you pick a lane (Christian, Buddhist, Hindu), Beckwith built Agape as 'trans-denominational,' welcoming all traditions and none, centering on direct spiritual experience rather than inherited belief. He also pioneered 'Life Visioning' as an alternative to goal-setting.
twoWorlds: New Thought Christianity meets Eastern meditation and visionary practice. He was raised without a strong religious background, had a spontaneous spiritual awakening in his twenties, then built a spiritual community that blends affirmative prayer from New Thought with meditation, chanting, and practices drawn from Buddhism, Hinduism, and mystical Christianity.
stupidSimplicity: You don't attract what you want — you attract what you are.
remarkableResult: Grew Agape from a living room prayer group in 1986 to over 10,000 local members and 1 million+ online followers across 212 countries. Featured in The Secret. Spoke at the UN General Assembly. Co-founded Association for Global New Thought, hosting conferences with the Dalai Lama.

name: Michael Singer
ruleBreak: Rejected the idea that spiritual depth and worldly success are incompatible. After a deep inner awakening during his doctoral program, he went into seclusion for yoga and meditation, built a forest ashram (Temple of the Universe) in 1975, then — while still living as a recluse yogi — created a software company that became worth billions. He proved you can be a monk and a CEO simultaneously.
twoWorlds: Reclusive yogi and meditation practitioner meets software entrepreneur and CEO. He was living in the woods doing deep meditation while simultaneously building Medical Manager, a healthcare software platform that was acquired by WebMD in a deal valued at roughly $5 billion. A forest hermit who built enterprise software.
stupidSimplicity: Stop listening to the voice inside your head — you are the one who hears it, not the one who speaks it.
remarkableResult: The Untethered Soul became a multi-million copy NYT bestseller, translated into dozens of languages. Founded Medical Manager, acquired by WebMD for ~$5 billion. Founded Temple of the Universe, a yoga and meditation center that has operated continuously since 1975 — over 50 years.

name: Mooji
ruleBreak: Rejected the idea that spiritual awakening is a long process requiring years of practice and preparation. While most teachers prescribed progressive paths (meditate daily for decades, study texts, accumulate merit), Mooji insists that what you are seeking is already here, already complete, and can be recognized right now through direct self-inquiry. He strips away all technique.
twoWorlds: Jamaican street artist and London art teacher meets Advaita Vedanta non-dual inquiry. Born in Port Antonio, Jamaica, raised in Brixton, London, he worked as a street portrait artist in the West End and taught at Brixton College before a meeting with Papaji in India in 1993 transformed him into a teacher of Ramana Maharshi's direct path of self-inquiry.
stupidSimplicity: You are not the person you think you are — find out who is watching.
remarkableResult: Built Monte Sahaja ashram in Portugal with 40-60 full-time residents. His YouTube channel has accumulated 76+ million views. Draws hundreds to silent retreats and satsangs worldwide, all built without any formal organization, marketing, or certification program — purely through word of mouth and free online videos.

name: Yung Pueblo
ruleBreak: Rejected the idea that spiritual teaching requires credentials, lineage, or authority. While most meditation teachers came from monasteries, ashrams, or psychology programs, Diego Perez was an Ecuadorian immigrant kid from Boston who fell into drugs in college, found Vipassana, and started posting raw, unpolished poetry about healing on Instagram. No lineage, no certification, no guru — just honest writing about inner work.
twoWorlds: Instagram poetry and social media meets deep Vipassana meditation practice. He combined the raw, confessional format of Instagram micro-poetry with insights drawn from 2+ hours of daily Vipassana practice, making ancient meditation wisdom feel like a text from a friend who gets it.
stupidSimplicity: Healing is the moment you stop running from yourself.
remarkableResult: Grew from anonymous Instagram poetry account to 2.4 million followers. #1 New York Times bestselling author. Sold nearly 2 million books translated into 25+ languages. All built from free Instagram posts — no paid ads, no publisher push, no traditional platform.

name: Sahara Rose
ruleBreak: Rejected the idea that Ayurveda must stay rooted in traditional Indian aesthetics and language to be authentic. While Ayurvedic practitioners insisted on Sanskrit terminology, traditional preparations, and 5,000-year-old formulations, Sahara Rose repackaged it with modern branding, plant-based recipes, and the concept of 'dharma' (purpose) as a lifestyle framework for millennials.
twoWorlds: Ancient Ayurvedic medicine meets modern digital media and millennial wellness culture. She taught health and sanitation in Indian slums where she discovered Ayurveda, then translated that ancient system through the lens of Instagram aesthetics, podcast culture, and contemporary plant-based cooking to make it accessible to a generation that had never heard of doshas.
stupidSimplicity: Your body already knows what it needs — Ayurveda just gives you the language to listen.
remarkableResult: Deepak Chopra called her 'a leading voice for the millennial generation into the new paradigm shift' and wrote the foreword to her books. Hosts the #1 spirituality podcast on iTunes (Highest Self Podcast) with 25+ million downloads. Keynote speaker at Google and Facebook. Featured as nutrition speaker for Michelle Obama's Let's Move campaign at Harvard Medical School.

name: Sam Harris
ruleBreak: Rejected the idea that meditation requires any spiritual or religious framework. While every other meditation teacher came wrapped in Buddhism, Hinduism, or New Age philosophy, Harris — a neuroscientist and outspoken atheist — stripped meditation down to a secular investigation of consciousness, arguing you can have the deepest contemplative insights without believing in anything supernatural.
twoWorlds: Academic neuroscience and militant atheism meets serious contemplative practice (Dzogchen and Advaita Vedanta). He has a PhD in neuroscience from UCLA and wrote bestselling books attacking religion, while simultaneously having spent years in silent retreat with Buddhist and Advaita masters. A committed meditator who thinks most of what meditators believe is nonsense.
stupidSimplicity: There is no self to find — just look for the one who is looking, and notice it isn't there.
remarkableResult: Built the Waking Up app to $700K+ monthly revenue. Multiple New York Times bestselling books. His TED talks and podcast reach millions. Made rigorous, non-dual meditation practice accessible to a secular audience that would never set foot in an ashram or monastery.

name: Seane Corn
ruleBreak: Rejected the idea that yoga stops at the mat. While the Western yoga industry focused on flexibility, fitness, and studio aesthetics, Seane Corn argued that yoga without social action is spiritual bypassing. She co-founded Off the Mat, Into the World to train yoga teachers in activism, taking them to Cambodia, South Africa, and Uganda to confront sex trafficking, HIV/AIDS, and poverty.
twoWorlds: Nightclub culture and addiction recovery meets yoga activism and social justice. She grew up borderline atheist in New Jersey, moved to New York at 17, worked in nightclubs (including Life Cafe with future Jivamukti co-founder David Life), struggled with addiction, then found yoga and turned it into a vehicle for frontline humanitarian work.
stupidSimplicity: What you do on the mat is practice for what you do in the world.
remarkableResult: Co-founded Off the Mat, Into the World, training thousands of yoga teachers in activism and leadership. Named National Yoga Ambassador for YouthAIDS. Received the Humanitarian Award from the Smithsonian Institution and the Global Green International Environmental Leadership Award.

name: Sri Sri Ravi Shankar
ruleBreak: Rejected the idea that powerful breathwork and meditation techniques must remain exclusive to advanced spiritual seekers. While most pranayama and kriya practices were guarded within lineages and required years of preparation, Sri Sri created Sudarshan Kriya — a specific rhythmic breathing technique — and made it available to anyone through a standardized weekend course, bypassing the traditional guru-disciple gatekeeping.
twoWorlds: Ancient Vedic spiritual traditions meets modern mass-scale organizational management. He studied under Maharishi Mahesh Yogi (Transcendental Meditation), then built his own foundation with the operational scale and franchise-like consistency of a global corporation, standardizing sacred practices into repeatable, teachable weekend courses delivered identically across 180 countries.
stupidSimplicity: When you attend to the rhythm of your breath, your mind settles and your nature is joy.
remarkableResult: Art of Living Foundation operates in 180 countries, with programs that have touched over 370 million people. Sudarshan Kriya, conceived during a 10-day silence in 1982, is now one of the most widely practiced breathing techniques on Earth. Multiple Nobel Peace Prize nominations.

name: Thich Nhat Hanh
ruleBreak: Rejected the separation between meditation and daily life. While Buddhist monasticism traditionally meant withdrawal from the world, Thich Nhat Hanh created 'engaged Buddhism,' insisting that mindfulness must be practiced while walking, eating, washing dishes, and confronting war — not only on a cushion. He also rejected taking sides in the Vietnam War, which got him exiled from his own country.
twoWorlds: Vietnamese Zen monasticism meets Western social activism and peace work. He was a monk ordained at 16 who became a peace activist during the Vietnam War, bridging centuries-old Zen practice with Martin Luther King Jr.'s nonviolent movement. King nominated him for the Nobel Peace Prize in 1967.
stupidSimplicity: Wash the dishes to wash the dishes — not to get them done.
remarkableResult: Published over 100 books selling millions of copies worldwide. Founded Plum Village in France (1982), now part of a network of 11 practice centers and 1,000+ local sanghas worldwide. Nominated for the Nobel Peace Prize by Martin Luther King Jr. Arguably did more than any single person to bring mindfulness into mainstream Western culture.

name: Radha Agrawal (Daybreaker)
ruleBreak: Rejected the idea that ecstatic communal dance requires alcohol, darkness, and late nights. While the entire nightlife industry was built on the premise that people need substances and 2am energy to let loose on a dance floor, Agrawal proved that sober dancing at 6am with green juice and a 'hugging committee' could fill venues that nightclubs couldn't.
twoWorlds: Nightclub entrepreneurship meets wellness and sober morning culture. She invested in a New York nightclub, became disillusioned by the toxic aspects of nightlife, then flipped the entire model: same DJ-quality music, same communal euphoria, but at sunrise, sober, with yoga warm-ups and communal intention-setting instead of bottle service.
stupidSimplicity: You don't need alcohol to feel alive — you just need to dance before the sun comes up.
remarkableResult: Grew Daybreaker from a 150-person experiment in 2013 to 800,000+ community members across events on all seven continents. Filled the Sydney Opera House, the Smithsonian, and the 102nd floor of One World Trade Center. Opened a nine-date stadium tour with Oprah in 2020. Bootstrapped to a seven-figure business.

name: Jeff Krasno (Wanderlust)
ruleBreak: Rejected the idea that yoga and wellness are quiet, solitary, indoor activities. While the yoga world was studio-bound and the music festival world was party-bound, Krasno merged them into a single multi-day outdoor experience — yoga by day, live music by night — creating a category that didn't exist before: the mindful festival.
twoWorlds: Music entertainment production meets yoga and mindful living. He was running a music entertainment company in lower Manhattan when his wife Schuyler Grant opened a yoga studio upstairs from his office. After witnessing yoga retreats' transformative power, he combined his event production expertise with the practice of yoga to create the world's largest yoga festival.
stupidSimplicity: Wellness isn't something you do alone in a room — it's something you experience together in nature.
remarkableResult: Grew Wanderlust from 3,000 attendees at the first festival in 2009 to 130,000+ annual guests across 70+ events in 16 countries. Tripled attendance in year two (to 13,000), then scaled to 28 international markets by 2016. Later founded Commune, extending the model into digital community and education.

name: Meghan Pappenheim (Yoga Barn)
ruleBreak: Rejected the idea that a yoga studio must be a single-discipline, single-room space. While yoga studios worldwide were small, single-style operations, Pappenheim built The Yoga Barn in Ubud as a multi-studio wellness campus — yoga, dance, meditation, healing, Ayurveda, colonics, organic food, and guesthouses — turning a yoga studio into a full ecosystem and destination.
twoWorlds: New York event production and entrepreneurship meets Balinese healing culture and Tri Hita Karana philosophy. She grew up in New York, started throwing international trips and parties at 17, worked for a travel agent in high school, then married a Balinese man and embedded herself in Ubud's traditional healing community, combining Western event-production savvy with Balinese spiritual infrastructure.
stupidSimplicity: Build the container and the community will come — make it big enough for every kind of seeker.
remarkableResult: Grew The Yoga Barn from two studios in 2007 to eight studios offering 20+ classes daily, making it the largest yoga studio complex in Indonesia. Co-created the BaliSpirit Festival (2008), now drawing 10,000+ visitors from 60+ countries annually. Spawned sister festivals in Hawaii, New Zealand, Ibiza, Mexico, Byron Bay, and Portugal.

name: Larry Harvey (Burning Man)
ruleBreak: Rejected the idea that art and community need institutions, curators, or audiences. While the art world ran on galleries, critics, and spectatorship, Harvey created Burning Man on the principle that everyone is a participant and nothing is for sale. He codified 10 principles including radical self-reliance, gifting, decommodification, and leaving no trace — building a temporary city with no spectators, no advertising, and no transactions.
twoWorlds: Countercultural bohemian artist meets urban planner and philosophical architect. He grew up on a farm outside Portland, moved to San Francisco, and burned a wooden effigy on Baker Beach in 1986 after a painful breakup. Then spent the next 30 years turning that cathartic act into a philosophical framework for participatory culture, designing a 70,000-person temporary city in the desert governed by 10 self-organizing principles.
stupidSimplicity: No spectators — everyone participates, nothing is for sale.
remarkableResult: Grew Burning Man from a bonfire on Baker Beach with a handful of friends (1986) to a 73,000-person temporary city in the Black Rock Desert. Spawned 100+ regional events in 20+ countries. Created a cultural movement that influenced Silicon Valley, the art world, and festival culture worldwide. The 10 Principles became a governance model studied by organizational theorists.

name: Gabby Bernstein
ruleBreak: Rejected the idea that spiritual teachers need to be older, polished, and past their struggles. At 25, while most spiritual authorities were grey-haired and composed, she started teaching A Course in Miracles openly as a recovering cocaine addict from the nightclub world, making her messy recovery story the credential rather than hiding it.
twoWorlds: New York nightclub PR and cocaine addiction meets A Course in Miracles and 12-step recovery. She was a nightlife publicist partying her way through New York's club scene before getting sober in 2005, then fused the energy and hustle of nightclub promotion with the forgiveness teachings of a dense 1970s channeled spiritual text, packaged for millennials on social media.
stupidSimplicity: The universe has your back — fear is a choice, and you can choose again right now.
remarkableResult: Named by Oprah as a 'next-generation thought leader.' The Universe Has Your Back sold 1M+ copies. Ten bestselling books. Co-hosted the Guinness World Records' largest guided meditation with Deepak Chopra. Named to Oprah's SuperSoul 100.

name: Jay Shetty
ruleBreak: Rejected the idea that ancient monastic wisdom is incompatible with modern digital media. While traditional monks stayed in ashrams and social media was considered spiritually trivial, Shetty lived as a Hindu monk in India for three years, then deliberately brought that training to Instagram and YouTube with cinematic production quality, treating social media as a legitimate distribution channel for genuine wisdom.
twoWorlds: Hindu monastic training meets viral social media content production. He was a 22-year-old from North London who left everything to live as a Vedic monk in India for three years, sleeping on the floor, meditating for hours, and studying ancient texts, then came back and applied storytelling and video production craft to translate that experience for the smartphone generation.
stupidSimplicity: Think like a monk — train your mind to find calm, purpose, and meaning in everything.
remarkableResult: 65 million social media followers. 64 million podcast downloads in year one of 'On Purpose.' Became Will Smith's personal spiritual adviser. Think Like a Monk became a #1 New York Times bestseller. Created one of the largest purpose-driven media platforms in the world from zero traditional credentials.

name: Esther Perel
ruleBreak: Broke the most sacred rule in therapy: confidentiality as a wall between the session room and the public. While every therapist kept sessions private, Perel recorded real couples therapy sessions — raw, unscripted, with real people's real problems — and published them as a podcast. She also challenged the therapeutic consensus that infidelity is purely destructive, arguing it can be a portal for growth.
twoWorlds: Children-of-Holocaust-survivors identity and European multilingual culture meets American couples therapy. She grew up in Antwerp above her family's clothing shop, daughter of two concentration camp survivors who 'chose to live, not just to not die.' She speaks nine languages fluently and brought a European sensibility about eroticism, pleasure, and the complexity of desire into an American therapy culture that moralised about monogamy.
stupidSimplicity: The quality of your relationships determines the quality of your life.
remarkableResult: TED talks with 30+ million combined views. 'Where Should We Begin?' became one of the most listened-to podcasts globally. 'Mating in Captivity' translated into nearly 30 languages. Named by the New York Times as the most important game-changer in sexuality and relationships since Dr. Ruth.

name: Rupert Spira
ruleBreak: Rejected the idea that non-duality is an abstract philosophy you intellectually understand. While most non-dual teachers gave talks that left people conceptually convinced but experientially unchanged, Spira uses guided meditations and precise, Socratic questioning to lead people to a direct recognition of awareness in real time during the conversation — making non-duality an immediate experience rather than a belief.
twoWorlds: World-class studio pottery and ceramics meets Advaita Vedanta non-dual inquiry. For 30+ years he was a celebrated potter whose work is in the Victoria and Albert Museum, known for incising poetry into glazed vessels. He studied with Francis Lucille, then closed his pottery studio in 2013 to teach non-duality full-time, bringing a craftsman's precision and aesthetic sensibility to the communication of formless awareness.
stupidSimplicity: You are not a person having an experience of awareness — you are awareness having an experience of being a person.
remarkableResult: YouTube channel with 76+ million views and 640K+ subscribers, making him arguably the most-watched living non-duality teacher. Work exhibited in the Victoria and Albert Museum and the Sainsbury Centre. Published multiple bestselling books on non-duality. Leads retreats and online gatherings that draw thousands from around the world.

name: Vinn Marti (Soul Motion)
ruleBreak: Rejected the idea that conscious dance must be either a free-form ecstatic release (like 5Rhythms or ecstatic dance) or a structured technique class. While the conscious dance world split into chaos-or-choreography, Marti created Soul Motion as a 'third way' — a practice with enough structure to build skill and mastery, but enough freedom that every dance is a genuine improvisation. He treats movement as a conversation, not a performance or a catharsis.
twoWorlds: Classical modern dance training meets New Thought Christianity and meditation. Raised in the Bronx, his mother coined 'Soul Motion' for him at age 8. He trained in ballet, jazz, and modern dance, then wove in New Thought spiritual practice and meditation, creating a conscious dance form rooted in both technical discipline and contemplative presence rather than pure spontaneity.
stupidSimplicity: Keep your soul in motion — dance is not what you do, it is who you are.
remarkableResult: LOW_CONFIDENCE — Vinn Marti has been teaching movement for over 35 years and Soul Motion is taught by certified teachers across the US, Europe, Latin America, Australia, Japan, and Iceland. However, specific metrics (number of certified teachers, total students, revenue) are not publicly documented in verifiable sources.

name: DJ Taz Rashid
ruleBreak: Rejected the idea that a DJ belongs in a nightclub and a yoga class needs quiet meditation music. While DJs worked after midnight and yoga teachers played gentle ambient tracks, Taz Rashid brought live DJing with deep house, world music, and bass directly into yoga classes and meditation events, proving that a DJ could serve the practice rather than distract from it.
twoWorlds: Bangladeshi immigrant and corporate recruiter meets live-instrument yoga DJ. Born in Dhaka, raised in America, he worked corporate jobs in hotels, real estate, and university recruiting before getting laid off in 2011 and pivoting to music. He plays guitar, keyboard, Native American flute, didgeridoo, and hand percussion, blending them with DJ sets that merge devotional music with 80s/90s pop remixes for yoga audiences.
stupidSimplicity: The right music doesn't distract from the practice — it IS the practice.
remarkableResult: LOW_CONFIDENCE — DJ Taz Rashid has been a fixture at Wanderlust, Bhakti Fest, Bali Spirit Fest, Yoga Journal Conference, and other major wellness festivals since 2011, and has shared stages with Xavier Rudd, Michael Franti, and Trevor Hall. At one Wanderlust Chicago event, 700 people signed up for his newsletter in a single day. However, specific metrics (total audience size, revenue, number of events) are not independently verifiable.

name: Meghan Currie
ruleBreak: Rejected the idea that yoga must fit neatly into a named style or lineage. While yoga teachers aligned with Ashtanga, Iyengar, Vinyasa, or Anusara, Currie blended them all with dance, somatics, and raw emotional expression into something unclassifiable — intuitive, sensual, slow-fluid movement that looks more like contemporary dance than any yoga tradition. She treated the practice as art, not exercise.
twoWorlds: Contemporary dance and visual art meets yoga and somatic healing. She started practicing Ashtanga at 19 in Costa Rica, studied Anusara alignment, then mashed all styles together with dance-like movement and painting (she is also a visual artist). She overcame anxiety, depression, eating disorders, and addiction through this practice, bringing a vulnerability and artistic sensibility that feels more like performance art than a yoga class.
stupidSimplicity: Tiny consistent practices rewire everything — micro-evolution, not revolution.
remarkableResult: LOW_CONFIDENCE — Her 'Mad Love' yoga video went viral with 1M+ YouTube views. 143K Instagram followers. Leads sold-out retreats and teacher trainings worldwide (Mallorca, Salento, etc.). Created the Micro Evolution Method and Isabelle Moon ethical yogawear. However, specific business metrics and revenue numbers are not publicly available.
